title: Loops and Repetition
subtitle: How Your Dashboard Renders 10 Lesson Cards Without Writing 10 Times
description: Master for, while, do...while, forEach, for...of, break, continue - and how your dashboard uses lessons.forEach to create 10 cards, and why loops prevent code repetition.

blocks.text: PAGE 1: Why Loops? Your Dashboard Has 10 Lessons - Don't Repeat Code!

Hey friend! Imagine you have 10 lessons. Without loops, you would write createLessonCard for lesson 1, then copy paste for lesson 2, then for lesson 3... 10 times same code! If you need to change card design, you change 10 places - nightmare!

Your dashboard does NOT repeat. It has lessons array with 10 objects [{id:1, title:'Intro'}, {id:2, title:'Variables'},...] and then lessons.forEach(lesson => { grid.appendChild(createLessonCard(lesson, completed)) }) - ONE loop renders all 10 cards! Change card design once in createLessonCard, all 10 cards update automatically.

Loop = repeat same code many times with different data. Your dashboard loop: For each lesson in lessons array, create card and append to grid. 10 lessons = loop runs 10 times, each time lesson variable is different lesson object.

Without loops, your dashboard HTML would have 3000 lines instead of 300! Loops are DRY - Don't Repeat Yourself - most important principle. Today you master 5 loop types and see your dashboard's exact forEach loop.
Real life loops: For each user in users, send email. For each lesson, check if completed. While loading, show spinner. For each XP, add to total. Loops everywhere in your dashboard and all apps.

blocks.text: PAGE 2: for Loop - The Classic Counter

for loop has 3 parts: for (initialization; condition; increment) { code }. Initialization runs once at start: let i = 0. Condition checked each iteration: i < lessons.length - if true, run code, if false, stop loop. Increment after each iteration: i++ means i = i + 1.

Example from your dashboard: for (let i = 0; i < lessons.length; i++) { create card for lessons[i] }. i starts 0, condition 0 < 5 true, create card for lessons[0], i++ => i=1, condition 1 <5 true, create card for lessons[1]... until i=5, 5<5 false, stop. Loop runs 5 times for 5 lessons.

i is index - position in array. Array indexes start 0: lessons[0] is first lesson, lessons[1] second, lessons[4] fifth. lessons.length is 5, but last index 4 because start 0. So condition i < length not i <= length, otherwise i=5 lessons[5] undefined!

Your dashboard could use for loop but uses forEach which is cleaner - no need to manage i index manually. But for loop important to understand, and useful when you need index or need to skip or break.

blocks.text: PAGE 3: forEach - Your Dashboard's Favorite Loop

forEach is array method that loops through each element and calls function for each. Your dashboard uses it: lessons.forEach(lesson => { grid.appendChild(createLessonCard(lesson, completed)) }) - for each lesson in array, create card and append.

forEach is cleaner than for loop - no need to manage i index, no risk of off-by-one error (i <= length vs i < length). It automatically gives you lesson element, not index. For rendering, forEach is perfect.

forEach takes callback function: lessons.forEach(function(lesson) {... }) or arrow: lessons.forEach(lesson => {... }). Callback receives element, index, array: forEach((lesson, index, array) => { console.log(index, lesson.title) }). Your dashboard uses only lesson param, not index.

Limitation: forEach cannot break or continue easily - it always loops all elements. For loop can break to stop early or continue to skip. Your dashboard renders all lessons, so forEach fine. If you need to stop when found lesson, for loop with break better.

Your exact dashboard code: lessons.forEach(lesson => { grid.appendChild(createLessonCard(lesson, completed)) }) - lessons is array of 10, forEach runs 10 times, each time lesson is different object {id:1, title:'Intro'}, createLessonCard creates article element, appendChild adds to grid div, grid added to lessonContainer.

blocks.text: PAGE 4: while and do...while - Loops with Condition at Start or End

while loop checks condition first, then runs code if true, repeats while condition true. Example: while (loading) { show spinner } - while loading true, show spinner, when loading false, stop. Your dashboard could use while for retry logic: while (retries < 3 &&!data) { try fetch }.

do...while checks condition after running code once - guarantees code runs at least once even if condition false initially. Example: do { ask for password } while (password incorrect) - asks at least once, then repeats while incorrect.

Your dashboard uses forEach for rendering because you know array length and want to render all. while useful when you don't know how many iterations - like while user has not completed course, keep showing next lesson. do...while useful for user input validation.

Infinite loop danger: while (true) {... } never stops, crashes browser! Always ensure condition becomes false eventually, or have break inside. Your dashboard's while would need increment or condition change inside loop.

blocks.question: Q1: You have lessons array with 5 lessons. You write for (let i = 0; i <= lessons.length; i++) { console.log(lessons[i].title) }. What happens on last iteration? Tricky off-by-one!
options: Logs 5 lessons plus undefined error on last iteration - because indexes 0-4 for 5 lessons, length is 5, i <= length means i goes 0,1,2,3,4,5 - when i=5, lessons[5] undefined, lessons[5].title throws TypeError: Cannot read property title of undefined. Should be i < length not i <= length. Your dashboard uses forEach which avoids this off-by-one bug automatically
blocks.correctFeedback: Exactly! Off-by-one bug - <= length goes one beyond last index. < length correct. forEach avoids index management, no off-by-one risk - your dashboard's forEach is safer!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Array length 5, indexes 0-4. i <= 5 means i=5 last iteration, lessons[5] undefined (no element at index 5),.title throws error. Should be i < length (0-4) or i <= length-1. forEach avoids this by giving element directly, no index to mess up.
blocks.reasoning: Off-by-one error - <= vs < with length - common bug, forEach prevents it.

blocks.text: PAGE 5: for...of and for...in - Modern Loops

for...of loops through values of iterable like array: for (let lesson of lessons) { console.log(lesson.title) } - lesson is value directly, not index. Cleaner than for loop when you need value not index. Your dashboard could use for...of instead of forEach: for (let lesson of lessons) { grid.appendChild(createLessonCard(lesson)) }.

for...in loops through keys/properties of object: for (let key in user) { console.log(key, user[key]) } - key is property name like xp, coins. Use for objects, not arrays! For arrays, for...in gives indexes as strings, not values, and includes inherited properties - buggy. Use for...of or forEach for arrays.
Your dashboard: lessons array, use for...of or forEach for values. user object {xp:120, coins:30}, use for...in to loop keys if you need to display all user stats dynamically.

blocks.question: Q2: You have lessons array. You use for...in to loop: for (let i in lessons) { console.log(lessons[i].title) }. It works but i is string '0' not number 0. What bug can this cause? And what should you use for arrays?
options: for...in gives index as string '0', not number 0, so i + 1 = '01' string concatenation not 1 math! And for...in includes inherited properties, not just array elements, can include unexpected keys. Should use for...of for values or for loop with number index or forEach - your dashboard uses forEach which gives value directly, no string index bug
blocks.correctFeedback: Yes! for...in index is string, '0'+1='01' bug! And includes inherited props. Use for...of or forEach for arrays - gives value directly, no index type bug. Your dashboard's forEach avoids this!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: for...in with array: i is '0' string, '0'+1='01' concatenation not 1! Also for...in loops inherited properties from prototype, not just array elements. Use for...of (values), for loop (number index), or forEach (value) for arrays. for...in is for objects.
blocks.reasoning: for...in with arrays gives string index and inherited props - bug source, use for...of/forEach for arrays.

blocks.text: PAGE 6: Break and Continue - Control Loop Flow

break stops loop entirely - exits loop, no more iterations. Your dashboard could use break to stop searching when found lesson: for (let i=0; i<lessons.length; i++) { if (lessons[i].id === searchId) { found = lessons[i]; break; } } - once found, break, no need to check rest.

continue skips current iteration and goes to next. Example: for each lesson, if lesson locked, skip rendering, continue to next lesson. Your dashboard could skip locked lessons: lessons.forEach? forEach cannot continue easily, but for loop: if (status==='locked') continue; render only non-locked.

forEach cannot break or continue with keywords - return in forEach only exits callback, not entire loop. To break/continue in forEach, need to use for loop or for...of which support break/continue. Your dashboard renders all lessons, so no need break, but if you search for specific lesson, for loop with break more efficient.

blocks.question: Q3: You have 100 lessons, you search for lesson id 5. You use forEach to loop all 100, vs for loop with break when found id 5 at index 4. Which is more efficient and why?
options: for loop with break more efficient - forEach always loops all 100 lessons even after finding id 5 at index 4, 95 extra iterations wasted. for loop with break stops at index 4 after finding, 5 iterations only, 95% faster for search. Your dashboard renders all lessons so forEach fine, but for search, for loop with break better
blocks.correctFeedback: Yes! forEach cannot break, always loops all. for loop with break stops early - efficient for search. Your dashboard renders all so forEach fine, but search should use for loop with break or find() method!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: forEach loops all 100 even after finding at index 4, 95 wasted iterations. for loop break stops at 5, only 5 iterations, much faster for search. Use for loop with break or Array.find() for search, forEach for rendering all.
blocks.reasoning: forEach vs for loop with break efficiency - forEach cannot break, always loops all, inefficient for search.

blocks.text: PAGE 7: Your Dashboard's Rendering Loop Deep Dive

Your dashboard's renderLessons function: lessonContainer.innerHTML = ''; create grid div with className lesson-grid, then lessons.forEach(lesson => { grid.appendChild(createLessonCard(lesson, completed)) }), then lessonContainer.appendChild(grid). This is 3 steps: clear container, loop to create cards and append to grid, append grid to container.

Why create grid first then append cards to grid, then grid to container, not directly append cards to container? Because grid is CSS grid with grid-template-columns: repeat(2, minmax(0, 1fr)) - 2 columns on desktop, 1 on mobile. If you append cards directly to container without grid div, no grid layout, cards stack vertically not in grid.

Performance: Appending to grid then grid to container is 1 reflow (browser recalculates layout once when grid appended), vs appending each card directly to container in loop would cause 10 reflows (one per append) - slower. Your dashboard's method is efficient - build in memory then append once.

blocks.question: Q4: Your dashboard does: grid = createElement('div'), lessons.forEach(lesson => grid.appendChild(createCard)), container.appendChild(grid). Why not container.appendChild(createCard) directly inside forEach loop? Performance trick!
options: Direct append in loop causes reflow for each card - 10 cards = 10 reflows (browser recalculates layout 10 times) slow. Grid method builds all cards in memory grid div, then appends grid once = 1 reflow, 10x faster! Also grid div has CSS grid-template-columns for 2-column layout, without grid div no grid layout. Your dashboard's method is efficient and correct layout
blocks.correctFeedback: Exactly! 1 reflow vs 10 reflows performance! And grid div needed for CSS grid layout. Your dashboard's build in memory then append once is pro efficient pattern!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Appending each card directly to container in loop triggers browser reflow (layout recalc) each time - 10 cards 10 reflows slow. Building grid in memory then appending grid once = 1 reflow fast. Also grid div has class lesson-grid with grid-template-columns CSS for 2 columns, needed for layout.
blocks.reasoning: DOM reflow performance - building in memory then single append is efficient - your dashboard's grid pattern.

blocks.text: PAGE 10: Summary & Tricky Final Questions

You mastered loops: for loop with initialization, condition, increment, index 0 to length-1, off-by-one bug <= vs <, break stops loop, continue skips iteration. forEach loops values, no index management, no off-by-one, but cannot break/continue - your dashboard uses forEach for rendering all 10 cards. while checks condition first may run 0 times, do...while runs at least once, both for unknown iterations like loading retries.

blocks.question: Q5: You have lessons array length 5, indexes 0-4. You write for (let i = 0; i <= lessons.length; i++) { console.log(lessons[i].title) }. What happens at i=5? Tricky off-by-one!
options: At i=5, lessons[5] undefined, lessons[5].title throws TypeError: Cannot read property title of undefined - because last index 4, length 5, <= length goes to 5 one beyond. Should be i < length not i <= length. Your dashboard's forEach avoids this by giving element directly, no index, no off-by-one
blocks.correctFeedback: Yes! Off-by-one - <= length goes beyond last index. < length correct. forEach avoids index, no off-by-one bug - your dashboard's forEach safer!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: Length 5, indexes 0-4. i <= 5 means i=5 last iteration, lessons[5] undefined,.title error. Should be i < 5 (0-4) or i <= 4. forEach gives lesson element directly, no index to mess up, avoids off-by-one.
blocks.reasoning: Off-by-one bug with <= vs < - common, forEach prevents it.

blocks.question: Q6: You have 100 lessons, search for id 5 at index 4. forEach loops all 100, for loop with break stops at 5 after finding. Which efficient? And can forEach break?
options: forEach cannot break with break keyword - return only exits callback not entire loop, still loops all 100, 95 wasted iterations. for loop with break stops at index 4 after finding, 5 iterations only, 95% faster for search. For rendering all, forEach fine, for search use for loop with break or find() - your dashboard renders all so forEach fine
blocks.correctFeedback: Exactly! forEach cannot break, always loops all. for loop break stops early efficient for search. Your dashboard renders all so forEach fine!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: forEach loops all 100 even after finding at index 4, 95 wasted. for loop break stops at 5, 5 iterations only, faster for search. forEach return only exits callback, not entire loop. Use for loop with break or Array.find() for search.
blocks.reasoning: forEach vs for loop break efficiency - forEach cannot break, inefficient for search.

options: for...in index is string '0', '0' + 1 = '01' concatenation not 1 math! Bug if you do i+1 for next lesson. Also for...in includes inherited properties. Should use for...of for values or for loop with number index or forEach - your dashboard uses forEach which gives value directly no string index bug
blocks.correctFeedback: Yes! String index bug '0'+1='01'! And inherited props. Use for...of/forEach for arrays - your dashboard's forEach avoids string index bug!
blocks.incorrectFeedback: for...in with array: i is '0' string, '0'+1='01' concatenation not 1! Also loops inherited prototype properties. Use for...of (values), for loop (number index), forEach (value) for arrays. for...in for objects.
blocks.reasoning: for...in with arrays string index bug and inherited props - use for...of/forEach for arrays.
